content: The Steering Group evaluated declared conflicts of interest to determine whether they were significant enough to compromise an individual’s ability to make objective judgments regarding evidence or recommendations. To ensure consistency, the group applied the criteria outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. Findings from declarations of interest (DOI) statements were managed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with WHO DOI guidelines and communicated to the experts involved. If a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant and unlikely to affect the guideline development process or its credibility, the expert was only required to declare the conflict during the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting, with no further action taken. A summary of DOI statements and the management of conflicts of interest is provided in Annex 2. To enhance public trust and transparency in WHO meetings involving expert advice for developing technical norms and standards, the names and brief biographies of individuals considered for participation in the guideline, along with the objectives of relevant meetings, were made public before the first planned meeting. This allowed time for public notice and comment. The priority questions and outcomes for the guideline were aligned with those of the 2016 WHO antenatal care (ANC) guideline. These questions and outcomes were informed by a comprehensive scoping exercise of existing clinical practice guidelines relevant to routine ANC, supplemented by a search of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews for key systematic reviews. Critical and important outcomes were identified through these reviews and a WHO-commissioned scoping qualitative review of what women want during pregnancy. This review revealed that pregnant women desire a positive pregnancy experience, defined as maintaining physical and sociocultural normality, ensuring a healthy pregnancy and baby, transitioning effectively to positive labor and birth, and achieving a positive motherhood. This overarching principle of a “positive pregnancy experience” became the foundation for ANC guideline recommendations. Evidence to support the recommendations was derived from multiple sources by methodologists working closely with the WHO Steering Group. An updated Cochrane systematic review served as the primary source of evidence on the effectiveness of oral antenatal multiple micronutrient supplements (MMS). Earlier versions of this review, based on randomized controlled trial (RCT) data synthesized using standardized Cochrane methodology, supported the 2016 ANC guideline recommendations. The updated RevMan file was retrieved from the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group and customized to reflect key comparisons, GDG-specified subgroup analyses, and outcomes relevant to the ANC guideline. Evidence was evaluated according to standard operating procedures approved by the WHO Steering Group, and evidence profiles (in the form of GRADE tables) were prepared, including assessments of evidence certainty for relevant comparisons. The GRADE approach was used to appraise the certainty of quantitative evidence, with outcomes rated as “high,” “moderate,” “low,” or “very low” based on established criteria. Evidence from Cochrane reviews was initially rated as “high certainty” due to its derivation from RCTs but was downgraded based on considerations such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Qualitative evidence was derived from qualitative evidence syntheses (QES) performed for the 2016 WHO ANC guideline and previously appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool. This tool assesses confidence in QES findings based on methodological limitations, adequacy of data, coherence, and relevance to the review question. The evidence was not re-graded for the updated recommendation. The WHO Steering Group supervised and finalized the preparation of the evidence summary and profile in collaboration with guideline methodologists, using the DECIDE framework. This framework systematically considers research evidence on interventions according to six criteria: effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. These criteria were populated with research evidence where available, and additional information was described in the “additional considerations” subsections. Certainty of graded evidence on intervention effectiveness was systematically interpreted in the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) frameworks following Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) Group guidance. GDG members and other participants were provided with the evidence summary in advance of the online GDG meeting held on December 4–5, 2019. During the meeting, under the leadership of the GDG chair, members reviewed, discussed, and made judgments on the impact of interventions for each EtD criterion. These judgments were summarized before finalizing the recommendation and remarks. The intervention could be recommended, not recommended, or recommended in specific contexts, such as rigorous research, targeted monitoring and evaluation, or other GDG-specified contexts. Following the GDG meeting, members of the WHO Steering Group, assisted by a methodologist, drafted a full guideline document to accurately reflect the deliberations and decisions of participants. A preliminary version of the document was sent electronically to participants and the External Review Group (ERG) for final review and technical comments. The Steering Group carefully evaluated peer reviewers’ input for inclusion in the guideline document and made revisions as needed. Further modifications after the GDG meetings and peer-review process were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. The document was then submitted for executive clearance following established WHO publication procedures. The WHO recommendation on antenatal MMS, adopted by the GDG, is detailed in this section along with its corresponding evidence summary. Evidence on the effectiveness of MMS is further elaborated in GRADE tables in Annex 3, along with selected forest plots. Additional remarks summarizing the GDG discussion are included below the recommendation to ensure clarity. The recommendation updates and supersedes the 2016 WHO ANC guideline recommendation.
